scenes.title: Git: Branching & Merging
scenes.narration: Branches let you develop new work in isolation, then merging folds that finished work back into the main line.

scenes.title: Why Branch
bullets: A branch is a safe, separate line of development that won't disturb main.
You can experiment freely and throw the branch away if it doesn't work out.
Teams work on many features in parallel without blocking each other.
scenes.narration: A branch is an independent workspace where you can build a feature without touching the stable main line. Because it is isolated, you are free to experiment and simply delete the branch if the idea fails. This is what lets a whole team pursue different features simultaneously without conflict.

scenes.title: The Branch Life Cycle
scenes.narration: The typical flow starts by creating a branch off main and committing your work there. When it is ready, you open a pull request so others can review it. After approval, the branch merges into main and is then deleted to keep the repository tidy.

scenes.title: Branching Commands
scenes.code:
git switch -c feature/clean-data   # create + switch
git add . && git commit -m "Clean nulls"
git switch main                    # back to main
git merge feature/clean-data       # fold it in
git branch -d feature/clean-data   # tidy up
scenes.narration: The switch command with -c creates a new branch and moves you onto it in one step. You commit your work there as usual, then switch back to main. Running git merge brings the feature's commits into main, and finally branch -d removes the branch now that its work is safely integrated.

scenes.title: Fast-Forward vs. Merge Commit
scenes.narration: If main has not changed since you branched, Git simply slides its pointer forward in a clean fast-forward. If main has also moved on, Git instead creates a dedicated merge commit that ties the two histories together. The merge commit preserves the fact that a branch existed, which many teams prefer for traceability.

scenes.text: Keep main deployable and do all real work on short-lived branches — small, frequent merges are far easier than giant ones.
scenes.narration: Protect main so it always works, and build everything on focused, short-lived branches. Merging often in small pieces avoids the pain of enormous, conflict-ridden merges.
